100.description: The server has received the request headers and the client should proceed to send the request body.
100.useCases: Used when a client needs to send a large request body. The server signals it is ready before the client sends the body, saving bandwidth if the server would reject the request anyway.

101.description: The requester has asked the server to switch protocols and the server has agreed to do so.
101.useCases: Commonly used when upgrading from HTTP to WebSocket. The client sends an Upgrade header and the server responds with 101 to confirm the protocol switch.

102.description: The server has received and is processing the request, but no response is available yet.
102.useCases: Used in WebDAV to prevent client timeouts on long-running operations. Signals that the server is working but hasn't finished yet.

103.description: Used to return some response headers before final HTTP message.
103.useCases: Allows browsers to start preloading resources while the server is still preparing a full response. Improves page load performance.

200.description: The request has succeeded. The information returned with the response is dependent on the method used in the request.
200.useCases: Standard response for successful GET, POST, PUT, PATCH requests. The response body contains the requested resource or result.

201.description: The request has been fulfilled and resulted in a new resource being created.
201.useCases: Returned after a successful POST request that creates a new resource. The Location header typically contains the URI of the new resource.

202.description: The request has been accepted for processing, but the processing has not been completed.
202.useCases: Used for asynchronous operations. The server accepted the request but will process it later, such as batch processing jobs.

203.description: The server is a transforming proxy that received a 200 OK from its origin, but is returning a modified version of the response.
203.useCases: Used by caching proxies or intermediaries that modify the response headers or body from an origin server.

204.description: The server successfully processed the request, but is not returning any content.
204.useCases: Returned for successful DELETE requests or PUT/PATCH when no body needs to be returned. Also used for auto-save operations.

205.description: The server successfully processed the request, but is not returning any content and requires the requester to reset the document view.
205.useCases: Instructs the client to reset the form or document after a submission. Similar to 204 but also clears user input.

206.description: The server is delivering only part of the resource due to a range header sent by the client.
206.useCases: Used for video streaming, resumable downloads, and paginated content delivery. The client requests a specific byte range using the Range header.

207.description: The message body that follows is by default an XML message and can contain a number of separate response codes.
207.useCases: Used in WebDAV for operations that affect multiple resources. Returns a status for each resource in the response body.

208.description: The members of a DAV binding have already been enumerated in a preceding part of the response.
208.useCases: Used in WebDAV to avoid repeatedly enumerating the internal members of multiple bindings to the same collection.

226.description: The server has fulfilled a GET request for the resource, and the response is a representation of the result of one or more instance-manipulations.
226.useCases: Used with HTTP delta encoding. The server returns a delta of the content rather than the full content.

300.description: The request has more than one possible response. The user-agent or user should choose one of them.
300.useCases: Used when a resource has multiple representations. The server provides a list of options for the client to choose from.

301.description: The URL of the requested resource has been changed permanently. The new URL is given in the response.
301.useCases: Use for permanent URL changes. SEO-friendly redirect that passes link equity. Browsers cache this redirect permanently.

302.description: The URI of requested resource has been changed temporarily. The client should continue to use the original URI.
302.useCases: Temporary redirect. Common for login redirects, A/B testing, and maintenance pages. Does not update bookmarks.

303.description: The server sent this response to direct the client to get the requested resource at another URI with a GET request.
303.useCases: Used after a POST/PUT/DELETE to redirect to a result page, following the Post/Redirect/Get pattern to prevent form resubmission.

304.description: Used for caching purposes. It tells the client that the response has not been modified, so the client can continue to use the same cached version of the response.
304.useCases: Returned when a client makes a conditional GET request using If-Modified-Since or If-None-Match headers and the resource hasn't changed.

307.description: The server sends this response to direct the client to get the requested resource at another URI with same method that was used in the prior request.
307.useCases: Like 302, but guarantees the HTTP method won't change. Used when temporarily moving a resource and the method must be preserved (e.g., POST stays POST).

308.description: The resource is now permanently located at another URI, specified by the Location: HTTP Response header.
308.useCases: Like 301, but preserves the HTTP method. Ideal for permanently moving API endpoints while keeping POST requests as POST.

400.description: The server could not understand the request due to invalid syntax.
400.useCases: Returned when the request has malformed syntax, invalid request message framing, or deceptive request routing. Common for invalid JSON bodies.

401.description: The client must authenticate itself to get the requested response.
401.useCases: Returned when accessing protected resources without authentication credentials, or when credentials are invalid. The client should send auth in the next request.

402.description: This response code is reserved for future use. Initial aim was for digital payment systems.
402.useCases: Used by some APIs to indicate quota exceeded or subscription required. Not part of the official HTTP spec but used in practice.

403.description: The client does not have access rights to the content. Unlike 401, the client's identity is known to the server.
403.useCases: The user is authenticated but lacks permission. Common for role-based access control. Also used to hide existence of resources.

404.description: The server can not find the requested resource. In the browser, this means the URL is not recognized.
404.useCases: The most well-known HTTP status. Used when a resource doesn't exist or to deliberately hide the existence of a resource (alternative to 403).

405.description: The request method is known by the server but is not supported by the target resource.
405.useCases: Returned when a POST is sent to a GET-only endpoint, or when trying to DELETE a read-only resource. The Allow header should list valid methods.

406.description: The server cannot produce a response matching the list of acceptable values defined in the request's content negotiation headers.
406.useCases: Returned when the Accept header requests a format (e.g., XML) that the server cannot provide.

407.description: Authentication is needed to be done by a proxy.
407.useCases: Similar to 401, but authentication must be performed against a proxy server before the request can proceed.

408.description: The server would like to shut down this unused connection. Some servers send this on idle connections.
408.useCases: Returned when a client takes too long to send the complete request. The server may close the connection or request a retry.

409.description: This response is sent when a request conflicts with the current state of the server.
409.useCases: Common when trying to create a duplicate resource, version conflicts in optimistic locking, or editing conflicts in collaborative systems.

410.description: This response is sent when the requested content has been permanently deleted from server, with no forwarding address.
410.useCases: More permanent than 404. Signals that the resource intentionally no longer exists. Helps search engines remove stale indexed pages.

411.description: Server rejected the request because the Content-Length header field is not defined and the server requires it.
411.useCases: Returned when sending a request body (e.g., POST) without specifying the Content-Length header, which the server requires.

412.description: The client has indicated preconditions in its headers which the server does not meet.
412.useCases: Used in conditional requests (If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since). Common for optimistic concurrency control in REST APIs.

413.description: Request entity is larger than limits defined by server.
413.useCases: Returned when uploading a file that exceeds the server's maximum allowed size, or when a request body is too large.

414.description: The URI requested by the client is longer than the server is willing to interpret.
414.useCases: Returned when a GET request URL is too long. Common when query parameters are used for large amounts of data instead of a POST body.

415.description: The media format of the requested data is not supported by the server.
415.useCases: Returned when sending application/xml to an endpoint that only accepts application/json, or sending an unsupported file type for upload.

416.description: The range specified by the Range header field in the request can't be fulfilled.
416.useCases: Returned for partial content requests when the requested byte range is out of bounds for the resource.

417.description: The expectation indicated by the Expect request header field can't be met by the server.
417.useCases: Returned when a client sends Expect: 100-continue but the server cannot or will not meet this expectation.

418.description: The server refuses the attempt to brew coffee with a teapot.
418.useCases: An April Fools' joke from RFC 2324. Used humorously or to signal that a resource refuses a particular type of request.

422.description: The request was well-formed but was unable to be followed due to semantic errors.
422.useCases: Used in REST APIs when validation fails (e.g., required fields missing, invalid field values). The structure is valid but the content is semantically incorrect.

423.description: The resource that is being accessed is locked.
423.useCases: Used in WebDAV when a resource is locked (e.g., checked out by another user) and cannot be modified.

424.description: The request failed due to failure of a previous request.
424.useCases: WebDAV status. Used when a batch operation fails because a dependency of the current operation failed.

425.description: Indicates that the server is unwilling to risk processing a request that might be replayed.
425.useCases: Used with TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT). Prevents replay attacks by refusing to process requests that may be replayed.

426.description: The server refuses to perform the request using the current protocol but might be willing to do so after the client upgrades to a different protocol.
426.useCases: Used to require the client to switch to a newer protocol, such as upgrading from HTTP/1.1 to HTTP/2.

428.description: The origin server requires the request to be conditional.
428.useCases: Forces clients to use conditional requests (ETags) to avoid lost-update problems in concurrent modifications of REST resources.

429.description: The user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time ("rate limiting").
429.useCases: API rate limiting. The Retry-After header indicates when the client can try again. Common in public APIs to prevent abuse.

431.description: The server is unwilling to process the request because its header fields are too large.
431.useCases: Returned when request headers (cookies, authorization tokens, custom headers) exceed the server's size limit.

451.description: The user agent requested a resource that cannot legally be provided.
451.useCases: Content blocked due to legal requirements such as GDPR, DMCA, court orders, or geo-based legal restrictions.

500.description: The server has encountered a situation it doesn't know how to handle.
500.useCases: Generic error for unhandled exceptions. Indicates a bug or unexpected condition on the server. Logs should be checked to diagnose the root cause.

501.description: The request method is not supported by the server and cannot be handled.
501.useCases: Returned when the server doesn't support a particular HTTP method at all. Different from 405 which means the method isn't supported for this specific resource.

502.description: The server, while working as a gateway to get a response needed to handle the request, got an invalid response.
502.useCases: Occurs when a reverse proxy (nginx, load balancer) receives an invalid response from the upstream application server. Often indicates the backend service crashed.

503.description: The server is not ready to handle the request. Common causes are a server that is down for maintenance or that is overloaded.
503.useCases: Used during scheduled maintenance or when the server is overloaded. Include Retry-After header to indicate when service will be restored.

504.description: The server is acting as a gateway and cannot get a response in time.
504.useCases: A reverse proxy didn't receive a timely response from the upstream server. Common with slow database queries or long-running operations.

505.description: The HTTP version used in the request is not supported by the server.
505.useCases: Returned when the server doesn't support the HTTP protocol version used in the request (e.g., server doesn't support HTTP/2).

506.description: The server has an internal configuration error: the chosen variant resource is configured to engage in transparent content negotiation itself.
506.useCases: Internal server misconfiguration. A variant resource is itself configured to participate in content negotiation, creating a circular reference.

507.description: The method could not be performed on the resource because the server is unable to store the representation needed to successfully complete the request.
507.useCases: WebDAV status. Returned when the server runs out of disk space or storage quota during a file upload or creation operation.

508.description: The server detected an infinite loop while processing the request.
508.useCases: WebDAV status. Detected when processing a Depth: infinity request that would create an infinite recursive loop.

510.description: Further extensions to the request are required for the server to fulfil it.
510.useCases: The server needs the client to use an extension to the HTTP protocol it announced in the response to process the request.

511.description: The client needs to authenticate to gain network access.
511.useCases: Used by network access control points (captive portals, Wi-Fi login pages) to redirect users to an authentication page before allowing internet access.

caseConverter.infoSnake: Common in Python, Ruby, and database column names. All lowercase with underscores.
caseConverter.infoKebab: Used in HTML attributes, CSS class names, and URL slugs. All lowercase with hyphens.

stringCounter.title: String Counter

stringCounter.inputPlaceholder: Paste or type your text here...

stringCounter.infoBytes: ASCII characters take 1 byte; accented and most European characters take 2; emoji can take 3–4 bytes.
stringCounter.infoUnique: Stop words (the, a, is, etc.) are excluded from the frequency count to show meaningful terms.
